title: Token Jumping in Planar Graphs has Linear Sized Kernels

snippets.content: Let G be a planar graph and I_s and I_t be two independent sets in G, each of size k. We begin with a "token" on each vertex of I_s and seek to move all tokens to I_t, by repeated "token jumping", removing a single token from one vertex and placing it on another vertex. We require that each intermediate arrangement of tokens again specifies an independent set of size k. Given G, I_s, and I_t, we ask whether there exists a sequence of token jumps that transforms I_s to I_t. When k is part of the input, this problem is known to be PSPACE-complete. However, it was shown by Ito, Kamiński, and Ono [4] to be fixed-parameter tractable. That is, when k is fixed, the problem can be solved in time polynomial in the order of G. Here we strengthen the upper bound on the running time in terms of k by showing that the problem has a kernel of size linear in k. More precisely, we transform an arbitrary input problem on a planar graph into an equivalent problem on a (planar) graph with order O(k).

Given a graph G, a subset of V(G) is independent if it induces no edges. In this paper we study the problem of transforming one independent set into another by a sequence of small changes. We model this as follows. to be fixed-parameter tractable. That is, when k is fixed, the problem can be solved in time polynomial in the order of G. In an excellent recent survey paper, Bousquet, Mouawad, Nishimura, and Siebertz [1] asked whether the problem admits a linear kernel. That is, given an arbitrary planar instance ISR-TJ(G, I_s, I_t), does there exist an equivalent instance on a (planar) graph G' where |V(G')| = O(k)? We answer their question affirmatively. (For a thorough history of independent set reconfiguration, and other related problems, we recommend [1].)
Theorem 1. On the class of planar graphs, ISR-TJ parametrized by k is fixed-parameter tractable with a kernel that has size linear in k.

Proof. Fix an input graph G, along with source and target independent sets, I_s and I_t, each of size k. We will show that either ISR-TJ(G, I_s, I_t) is trivially answered YES, or else ISR-TJ(G, I_s, I_t) is equivalent to a problem ISR-TJ(G', I_s, I_t), where G' is a subgraph of G and |V(G')| = O(k). Let X := I_s ∪ I_t and note that |X| ≤ 2k. For each Y ⊆ X, the X-projection class C_Y is defined by C_Y := { v ∈ V(G) s.t. N(v) ∩ X = Y }.

\[
C_1 := \bigcup_{\substack{Y \subseteq X \\ |Y| \leq 1}} C_Y \quad \text{and} \quad
C_2 := \bigcup_{\substack{Y \subseteq X \\ |Y| = 2}} C_Y \quad \text{and} \quad
C_3 := \bigcup_{\substack{Y \subseteq X \\ |Y| \geq 3}} C_Y.
\]
Claim 1. If |C_1| ≥ 4k, then the answer to ISR-TJ(G, I_s, I_t) is YES.

Proof. Assume |C_1| ≥ 4k. Since G[C_1] is planar, it is 4-colorable. By Pigeonhole, C_1 contains an independent set I_m (for middle) of size 4k / 4 = k. Starting with tokens on I_s, for each v ∈ I_s with a neighbor w_v ∈ I_m, move the token on v to some such w_v. Now move all remaining tokens (in an arbitrary order) to the unoccupied vertices of I_m. By symmetry, we can also move all tokens from I_t to I_m. Thus, the answer to ISR-TJ(G, I_s, I_t) is YES, as claimed.
Claim 2. |C_3| ≤ 8k.

Proof. First note that the number of sets Y with |Y| ≥ 3 and C_Y ≠ ∅ is less than 2|X|. To see this, we draw a plane graph G_X with vertex set X where each such set Y corresponds to a face of G_X. (Think of restricting G to X and one vertex v_Y in C_Y for each such Y. For each pair of vertices, u_i and u_j, that appear successively around v_Y, add edge y_i y_j, if it is not already present, following the path y_i v_Y y_j. Finally, delete each v_Y; and "assign" the resulting newly created face to Y.) By Euler's Formula, the resulting plane graph has at most 3|X| - 6 edges, so at most 2|X| - 4 faces. Since G is planar, it is K_3,3-free, so |C_Y| ≤ 2 for all such Y. Thus, |C_3| ≤ 2(2|X|) ≤ 4(2k).

An X-pair Y is a set {y', y''} such that y', y'' ∈ X and C_{y',y''} ≠ ∅. Let P denote the set of all X-pairs. As in the proof of Claim 2, we can show that |P| ≤ 3|X|. (Each X-pair corresponds to an edge of a plane graph with vertex set X.) We assume we are given a plane embedding of G. For each X-pair Y, this embedding induces a linear order on C_Y; intuitively, this order is "left-to-right", but there are subtleties, which we highlight below in Figure 1. Suppose Y = {y', y''}. Let H_Y := G[Y ∪ C_Y] - y'y''. Consider the outer face f_0. If f_0 contained at least three vertices of C_Y, then we could add a new vertex y''' to the interior of f_0, making it adjacent to all vertices on f_0. This would give a plane embedding of K_3,3 (with one part equal to {y', y'', y'''} and the other part contained in C_Y), a contradiction. So f_0 contains at most two vertices of C_Y. Further, since |f_0| ≥ 3 and y'y'' ∉ E(H_Y), in fact f_0 contains exactly two vertices in C_Y. Arbitrarily denote one of these z^ℓ and the other z^r (for left and right). We say z^ℓ is the leftmost vertex in C_Y. Deleting z^ℓ, we can repeat the argument on H_Y - z^ℓ. The new vertex on the outer face is now considered the "next-leftmost". Recursively, we can extend this ordering to all of C_Y. At some step in this process, we may transition from having one vertex of Y on the outer face to having two. However, at each step we will add exactly one new vertex of C_Y, and that new vertex will be the next in the linear order. Let N^{Int}(Y) := C_Y \ {z^ℓ, z^r}; this denotes the "interior" vertices in C_Y. For distinct Y_1, Y_2 ∈ P, we would like to move tokens in C_{Y_1} independently of those in C_{Y_2}. This is made possible by restricting ourselves to only moving tokens in N^{Int}(Y_1) and N^{Int}(Y_2), as confirmed by Claim 3.
Claim 3. If Y_1, Y_2 ∈ P, with Y_1 ≠ Y_2, and z_i ∈ N^{Int}(Y_i) for each i ∈ {1,2}, then z_1 z_2 ∉ E(G).
![Figure 0](data:image/jpeg;base64,...) [Embedded base64 image - Figure 0]
![Figure 1](data:image/jpeg;base64,...) [Embedded base64 image - Figure 1]

Proof. Since N^{Int}(Y_i) ≠ ∅, the leftmost and rightmost vertex in C_{Y_i} are distinct; call them z_i^ℓ and z_i^r. Denote Y_i by {y_i', y_i''}, for each i ∈ {1,2}. Let C_i := y_i' z_i^ℓ y_i'' z_i^r for each i ∈ {1,2}. Note that C_1 and C_2 might not be disjoint, but they intersect in at most one vertex; that is, |Y_1 ∩ Y_2| ≤ 1. Consider the regions with C_1 and C_2 as their boundaries; call them R_1 and R_2. Because C_1 and C_2 intersect at no more than one point, either R_1 and R_2 are disjoint or else one lies completely inside (topologically) the other; say R_1 lies inside R_2. In both cases, z_1 lies inside C_1, and z_2 lies outside it. Thus, z_1 z_2 ∉ E(G).

It is helpful to note, for each Y ∈ P, that G[C_Y] is a linear forest, since each z ∈ C_Y has edges only to (possibly) its predecessor and/or successor in the linear order. Let P_Big := {{y', y''} ∈ P s.t. N^{Int}(y', y'') has two non-adjacent vertices}.
Claim 4. Let G_{P_Big} be the subgraph of G induced by ∪_{Y ∈ P_Big} N^{Int}(Y). If G_{P_Big} has no independent set of size k, then |V(G)| ≤ 40k, so G is a linear kernel.

\[
\begin{aligned}
|\cup_{Y \in \mathcal{P}} C_Y| &\leq |\cup_{Y \in \mathcal{P}}(2 + |N^{\mathrm{Int}}(Y)|)| \\
&= 2|\mathcal{P}| + |\cup_{Y \in \mathcal{P} \setminus \mathcal{P}_{Big}} N^{\mathrm{Int}}(Y)| + |\cup_{Y \in \mathcal{P}_{Big}} N^{\mathrm{Int}}(Y)| \\
&\leq 2|\mathcal{P}| + (\sum_{Y \in \mathcal{P} \setminus \mathcal{P}_{Big}} 2) + |\cup_{Y \in \mathcal{P}_{Big}} N^{\mathrm{Int}}(Y)| \\
&\leq 2|\mathcal{P}| + 2|\mathcal{P}| + 2(k-1) \\
&\leq 4|\mathcal{P}| + 2(k-1) \\
&\leq 4(3(|X|)) + 2k \leq 12(2k) + 2k = 26k.
\end{aligned}
\]

Proof. ... Here (1) uses that N^{Int}(Y) is a linear forest (disjoint union of paths) for every Y ∈ P, that 2α(H) ≥ |V(H)| when H is a linear forest, and that α(H_1 + H_2 + ...) = Σ_i α(H_i), when H_1 + H_2 + ... is a disjoint union of linear forests. Claims 1 and 2 give |V(G)| = |X| + |C_1| + |C_2| + |C_3| ≤ 2k + 4k + 26k + 8k = 40k.
Claim 5. In every linear forest, every independent set of size k can be reconfigured to every other (in at most 2k steps).

Proof Sketch. We order the paths arbitrarily, and pick a "left end" for each. We now iteratively move each token on the first path as far left as possible, and then fill the remainder of the path with remaining tokens. We finish recursively on the remaining paths and tokens. This transforms an arbitrary independent set of size k to a canonical one, in at most k steps.

snippets.location: Construction of J_s, J_t and G'
snippets.content: Henceforth, we assume that G_{P_Big} contains an independent set of size k; call it J_m. We will form sets J_s and J_t (not necessarily independent, but each inducing a linear forest), each of size O(k), and form G' from G by deleting (∪_{Y ∈ P_Big} N^{Int}(Y)) \ (J_m ∪ J_s ∪ J_t). Clearly |V(G')| = O(k). So it remains to specify J_s and J_t, and to show that ISR-TJ(G', I_s, I_t) is equivalent to ISR-TJ(G, I_s, I_t). Let P^1 be the set of X-pairs with at most one vertex in I_s and let P^2 be the set of X-pairs with two vertices in I_s. To form J_s, start by including, for all Y ∈ P^1, each vertex in C_Y such that I_s contains at most one vertex of Y, up to the point (if it occurs) where J_s contains an independent set of size k that lies entirely in ∪_{Y ∈ P^1} N^{Int}(Y). If this point occurs, we are done forming J_s; so assume it does not. Now, we consider each Y ∈ P^2. For each such Y, add to J_s the leftmost and right vertex in C_Y as well as two vertices in N^{Int}(Y), if they exist, giving preference to a non-adjacent pair. Analogously, we construct J_t with I_t in the role of I_s.

snippets.content: Proof of size bounds. For each Y ∈ P^1, its contribution to a maximum independent set contained in ∪_{Y ∈ P^1} N^{Int}(Y) is α(G[N^{Int}(Y)]) ≥ |N^{Int}(Y)| / 2, because N^{Int}(Y) induces a linear forest. Since the size of such a set is at most k (by construction), we have |∪_{Y ∈ P^1} N^{Int}(Y)| ≤ 2 Σ_{Y ∈ P^1} α(G[N^{Int}(Y)]) ≤ 2k. Now |J_s ∪ J_t ∪ J_m| ≤ |J_s| + |J_t| + |J_m| ≤ 26k + 26k + k = 53k. Thus, |V(G')| ≤ |X| + |C_1| + |J_s ∪ J_t ∪ J_m| + |C_3| ≤ 2k + 4k + 53k + 8k = 67k.

ISR-TJ(G, I_s, I_t). For the latter, we will show that if in G we can move a token to a vertex absent from G', then in G' we can move all tokens from I_s to J_s ∪ J_m, and we can also move all tokens from I_t to J_t ∪ J_m. Since G[J_s ∪ J_t ∪ J_m] is a linear forest, by Claim 4 the answer to ISR-TJ(G', I_s, I_t) is YES. Lastly, we show that when we restrict G to G' the problem stays equivalent.
Claim 7. ISR-TJ(G', I_s, I_t) is equivalent to ISR-TJ(G, I_s, I_t).

Proof. Since G' ⊆ G, if the answer to ISR-TJ(G, I_s, I_t) is NO, then clearly the answer to ISR-TJ(G', I_s, I_t) is also NO. So it suffices to show that if the answer to ISR-TJ(G, I_s, I_t) is YES, then also the answer to ISR-TJ(G', I_s, I_t) is YES. Suppose that the answer to ISR-TJ(G, I_s, I_t) is YES, and let σ be a sequence of token jumps witnessing this. If each vertex appearing in σ is a vertex of G' then σ also witnesses that the answer to ISR-TJ(G', I_s, I_t) is YES. So assume that σ uses some vertex that is not in G'. Let z_s and z_t denote the first and last such vertex used by σ that are not in V(G'). We will show that (a) because z_s ∉ V(G'), we can move all tokens from I_s to vertices of J_s ∪ J_m. Similarly (b) because z_t ∉ V(G'), we can move all tokens from I_t to vertices of J_t ∪ J_m. The arguments are essentially identical, so it suffices to prove (a). Suppose that z_s ∈ ∪_{Y ∈ P^1} C_Y. What caused z_s to be absent from J_s? It is because J_s contains an independent set, call it J_1 of size k that lies entirely in ∪_{Y ∈ P^1} N^{Int}(Y). For each token on a vertex v with a neighbor w in J_1, we move the token to w. This cannot create any conflicts since J_1 is an independent set and is contained in ∪_{Y ∈ P^1} N^{Int}(Y). Now each vertex of J_1 has no neighbor with a token, so we can greedily move the remaining tokens to the unoccupied vertices of J_1. Thus, we are done if J_1 exists; so we assume it does not. Instead assume that z_s ∈ ∪_{Y ∈ P^2} C_Y. By our construction of G', since z_s ∉ V(G'), we know z_s ∈ ∪_{Y ∈ P_Big} N^{Int}(Y). Denote P_Big ∩ P^2 by {Y_1, ..., Y_a} in an arbitrary order, and denote Y_i by {y_i', y_i''} for each i. Since σ moves a token to z_s, at some earlier point σ moves a token off of some vertex in some Y_i. By symmetry, assume σ first moves a token off of y_1'. We show, by induction on i, that we can move all tokens off of ∪_{i=1}^a Y_i. Recall, for each i, that N^{Int}(Y_i) contains non-adjacent vertices that lie in J_m; call such a pair z_i' and z_i''. For the base case, we move the token on y_1'' to z_1'. For the induction step, we assume that no token appears on the closed neighborhood of z_{i-1}''. So we move a token from y_i' to z_{i-1}'' and then we move a token from y_i'' to z_i'. This finishes the induction proof. Once all tokens are removed from ∪_{i=1}^a Y_i, by Claim 4 we move all tokens on ∪_{i=1}^a {z_i', z_i''} to J_m. Finally, we greedily move all remaining tokens to J_m. Claim 7 finishes the proof of Theorem 1.
